sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
This paper presents a fixed-fixed folded spring as an alternative elastic element for beambased piezoelectric energy harvesting. In order to harvest energy from low frequency vibration in an optimal manner, the natural/operational frequencies of harvesters must be reduced to match low frequency input vibrations. Therefore, natural frequency reduction of vibrationbased energy harvesters is critical to maximize output power at low operational frequency. The mechanical optimization of cantilever-based piezoelectric energy harvesters is limited by residual stress-based beam curling that produced through microfabrication adding additional mechanical stiffness to the system. The fixed-fixed folded spring structure presented in this paper allows for increased effective beam length and residual stress relaxation, without out of plane beam curling to further reducing the natural frequency. Multiple designs of folded spring energy harvesters are presented to demonstrate the effect of important design parameters. It is shown that the folded spring harvesters were capable of harvesting electricity at low natural frequencies, ranging from $4 5 \mathrm { H z }$ to $3 6 6 7 \mathrm { H z }$ . Additionally, the harvesters were shown to be insensitive to microfabrication-based residual stress beam curling. The maximum power output achieved by the folded spring harvesters was $6 9 0 . 5 \mathrm { n W }$ at $2 2 6 . 3 \mathrm { H z }$ for a single harvesting element of an array, with a PZT layer thickness of $0 . 2 4 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The work presented in this paper demonstrates that the fixed-fixed folded spring can be used as a viable structural element for low frequency piezoelectric energy harvesting to take advantage of ambient vibrations found in low frequency applications.

Keywords: MEMS, piezoelectric energy harvesting, stiffness optimization, frequency response, microfabrication, geometric manipulation, folded spring, residual stress relaxation (Some figures may appear in colour only in the online journal)

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Energy harvesting is an important field in MEMS research. The introduction of energy harvesters into personal electronics, wireless sensors, and MEMS-based sensing platforms as a complimentary technology can allow for the extension of operational lifespan of traditional battery-based power schemes. Long term MEMS-based biomedical applications, such as MEMS-instrumented implants, are an attractive application for energy harvesting. In the case of biomedical applications, the ability to lengthen the battery lifespan of a MEMS-based sensing platform would increase the level of patient care. There are a variety of energy harvesting methods available including photovoltaic, micro fuel cells, thermoelectric, electromagnetic, electrostatic, and piezoelectric methods [1–5]. Of the vibration-based schemes, piezoelectric energy harvesters are more universally applicable with generally higher power densities than the other vibration-based methods [1, 2, 6]. Piezoelectric energy harvesting converts ambient vibrational energy into electricity via the piezoelectric effect [4, 7]. Low frequency ambient vibrations, including those produced by human motion, can occur on the order of $3 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ and less.

Piezoelectric harvesting can produce a reasonable amount of output power at low frequency, thus piezoelectric energy harvesting is an attractive technology for a variety of biomedical applications [8, 9]. Therefore, optimizing the dynamics of the structural element of the harvester is of great importance to reduce the natural frequency of the harvester to match human motion to generate maximum energy.

It has been shown in literature [4, 10] that the performance of piezoelectric energy harvesters is tied to the dynamic performance of the structural element used in the device. The operational frequency of the energy harvester should match the first natural frequency of the mechanical element of the energy harvester. This ensures that the maximum deflection and strain on the piezoelectric film is achieved at the operational frequency [4, 10]. Additionally, the natural frequency of the energy harvester should be as low as possible to ensure that the structure of the energy harvester will be actuated by ambient vibrations present in-situ [4, 10]. Therefore, it is critical that the natural/operational frequency of the harvester is optimized to maximize the strain applied to the piezoelectric elements to improve power output.

Cantilever-based energy harvesters are the most common piezoelectric-based energy harvesters found in literature due to their well-known dynamics, straightforward optimization, and ease of fabrication [4, 10–12]. There are two methods of reducing the natural frequency of the cantilever-based harvester systems: adding mass to the system or reducing the stiffness of the beam. The residual stress produced through microfabrication will cause a change in the “at-rest” state of the cantilever beam, manifesting as an out of plane displacement of the beam when released. This behaviour is length-dependant, increasing the residual stress-based out of plane curling at increased beam length. This initial displacement can artificially inflate the mechanical stiffness of the cantilever beam leading to an increase in natural frequency [13].

A folded fixed-fixed beam is suggested in this paper as an alternative to cantilevers as a structural element for piezoelectric energy harvesting. The folded structure of the beam allows for the relaxation of residual stress without out of plane displacement. If any mass suspended by the folded springs is allowed to rotate, the equal expansion and contraction of the individual beam segments will not cause any change to the mechanical stiffness [14–16]. The folded beam allows for a high degree of customization and natural frequency reduction leading to frequency reduction and matching, strain optimization, and increased power output. Folded beams are common structures used in planar and vertical comb drives [13] and are typically used as the mechanical elements in electrostatic-based energy harvesting [1, 2, 11, 17] and some electromagnetic-based energy harvesting [18]. There have been attempts in using advanced beam shapes, such as serpentine/coiled [19] and simple folded beams [20] to lower natural frequency and improve power output. The folded spring based harvester examined in this paper allows for the development of complex arrays of harvesting elements to further enhance the power output of an energy harvester while reducing the effects of fabrication-induced residual stress stiffening.

Two classes of energy harvesters will be produced in this study to explore this methodology. The first class of energy harvesters studied will focus on developing the microfabrication process flow and initial proof of concept of the fixed-fixed folded spring. The second class of energy harvesters will deal with the examination of complex arrays of folded spring energy harvesters and seismic masses that will further reduce the natural frequency and increase output energy. The performance of the each class of energy harvesters will be numerically and experimentally examined to identify the important geometric parameters of the folded spring and to determine the benefit of the folded spring methodology.

sections.heading: 2. Background and theory
sections.text:
Piezoelectric energy harvesters convert vibration induced strain to electricity via the piezoelectric effect. Piezoelectric materials have an inherent lack of inversion symmetry, which allows aligned electric dipoles to form within the material [13]. When the piezoelectric material is stressed, the electrons become mobile within the crystal, generating a potential difference, and hence a current flow [13, 21]. Of the available methods of vibration-based piezoelectric energy harvesting cantilever beam-based harvesting is the most popular [1]. The most typical configuration of beambased piezoelectric energy harvesting utilizes a cantilever beam with thin film PZT and a proof mass to convert the applied vibration into a mechanical strain applied to a piezoelectric element in the 31-mode [1, 7].

There are several design rules postulated by Roundy et al [4, 10, 11]. that give a general framework of the mechanical and electrical optimization of these devices. The critical design rules include matching the natural frequency of the harvester to the operational/input frequency of the vibration that the energy harvester is exposed to. Additionally, lowering both the natural and operational frequency of the system will increase the total output of the system. This can be seen by the analytical formulation shown below [10]:

$$
P = \frac { 1 } { 2 R } \times \frac { \left( \frac { 2 k _ { 3 1 } t _ { c } } { k _ { 2 } } \right) ^ { 2 } \frac { c _ { p } } { \varepsilon } A _ { i n } ^ { 2 } } { \left[ \frac { \omega _ { n } ^ { 2 } } { \omega R C _ { b } } - \omega \left( \frac { 1 } { R C _ { b } } + 2 \xi \omega _ { n } \right) \right] ^ { 2 } + \left[ \omega _ { n } ^ { 2 } \left( 1 + k _ { 3 1 } ^ { 2 } \right) + \frac { 2 \xi \omega _ { n } } { R C _ { b } } - \omega ^ { 2 } \right] ^ { 2 } }
$$

Where $R$ is the load resistance, $k _ { 3 1 }$ is the piezoelectric coupling coefficient, $t _ { c }$ is the thickness the piezoelectric ceramic, $k _ { 2 }$ is a geometric constant that relates average piezoelectric material strain to the tip deflection, $c _ { p }$ is the elastic constant of the piezoelectric ceramic, ε is the dielectric constant of piezoelectric material, $A _ { i n }$ is the input vibration amplitude, $\omega _ { n }$ is the resonance frequency of the generator, $\omega$ is the frequency of driving vibrations, $C _ { b }$ is the capacitance of the piezoelectric bimorph, and $\xi$ is the dimensionless damping ratio which represents the viscous loss from the system [10]. It can be seen from equation  (1), in order to provide a high power output, the mechanical behaviour of the harvester is equally important as the electrical behaviour. Therefore, to optimize the power output of the energy harvesters, assuming a matched operational and natural frequency, the highest power output will be achieved at the lowest natural frequency possible.

![](images/9eb213d44abb792baa5598b073405d6999c0d0c1754a4350f96a40917e05ca5f.jpg)  
Figure 1. One dimensional lumped mass/spring/damper system (left) with series and parallel configurations (right).

By expressing the dynamics of the piezoelectric energy harvester as a one-dimensional vibration problem, using series and parallel configurations of spring and damper elements, as shown in figure 1, it can be seen that the optimization of the frequency response can be accomplished by either reducing the mechanical stiffness and/or increasing the inertial mass.

As shown in figure  1, the piezoelectric energy harvester can be represented (with some assumptions) as a simple linear mass/spring/damper system, with effective masses $( m _ { e } )$ , spring stiffnesses $( k _ { e } )$ , damping $( c _ { e } )$ , displacement $( x )$ and applied forces $( F )$ . In the simplification in figure 1, the forces applied to the harvester represent the ambient vibration-based loading, and may be time or frequency varying. The effective masses/ stiffnesses/damping can be lumped using equations (2).

$$
{ \begin{array} { l } { { \boldsymbol { k _ { e , { \mathrm { p a r a l l e l } } } } = k _ { 1 } + k _ { 2 } + \ldots + k _ { n } } } \\ { { \boldsymbol { k _ { e , { \mathrm { s e r i e s } } } } = { \cfrac { 1 } { k _ { 1 } } } + { \cfrac { 1 } { k _ { 2 } } } + \ldots + { \cfrac { 1 } { k _ { n } } } } } \\ { { \boldsymbol { c _ { e , { \mathrm { p a r a l l e l } } } } = c _ { 1 } + c _ { 2 } + \ldots + c _ { n } } } \\ { { \boldsymbol { c _ { e , { \mathrm { s e r i e s } } } } = { \cfrac { 1 } { c _ { 1 } } } + { \cfrac { 1 } { c _ { 2 } } } + \ldots + { \cfrac { 1 } { c _ { n } } } } } \end{array} }
$$

Where, in equation (2) and figure 1, $k _ { n }$ is the stiffness of the nth spring element, and $c _ { n }$ is the damping of the nth damper. As can be seen by equations (2), the proper equation of spring/ damper systems must be chosen in order to properly represent the configuration of the system. The mechanical stiffness/ damping of the system can be simplified using parallel and series springs approximations discussed in equation  (2) according to the physical configuration of those elements. With these simplifications, the natural frequency and equation of motion of the lumped system is shown below:

$$
\begin{array} { c } { \displaystyle \omega _ { n } = \sqrt { \frac { k _ { e } } { m _ { e } } } } \\ { F = m _ { e } \ddot { x } + c _ { e } \dot { x } + k _ { e } x } \end{array}
$$

Increasing the mass of the system is the preferred method of optimization of cantilever-based energy harvesting in literature, due to the difficulty of fabricating mechanically stable low stiffness that are insensitive to detrimental residual stresses. However, as seen in equations (3), increasing mass alone cannot truly give an optimized, minimized natural frequency. Additionally, there are practical limitations with increasing the mass of the harvester to lower the natural frequency, such as the volume of the mass that could be added to the harvester. Alternatively, the stiffness of the mechanical spring element can be reduced to provide natural frequency reduction. For cantilever based systems, the stiffness of the energy harvester can be expressed by equation (4 [13]):

$$
k = \frac { E W H ^ { 3 } } { 4 L ^ { 3 } }
$$

Where $k$ is the beam stiffness, $E$ is the Young’s Modulus, $W$ is the beam width, $H$ is the beam thickness, and $L$ is the length of the cantilever beam. The typical methodology of reducing the stiffness of cantilever-based harvesters involves increasing the length or decreasing the thickness of the cantilever. When the thickness of the beam is reduced, resulting in a “thin” structure $( H < < W )$ , the beam curling due to residual stress relaxation of the cantilever can become accentuated with increased length [13]. This behaviour directly opposes any beam length optimization of the cantilever harvester.

In order to overcome this challenge, while reducing the natural frequency of the harvester, a folded spring will be applied to the energy harvester. The second fixed beam end prevents the curling-based stress relaxation seen with cantilever beams, therefore residual stresses can occur. Using energy methods, the complete non-linear force/deflection relation of the fixedfixed beam can be derived, as shown in equation (5) [13].

$$
F = \left\{ { \left( \frac { \pi ^ { 2 } } { 2 } \right) } { \left[ \frac { \sigma W H } { L } \right] } + { \left( \frac { \pi ^ { 4 } } { 6 } \right) } { \left[ \frac { E W H ^ { 3 } } { L ^ { 3 } } \right] } \right\} x + { \left( \frac { \pi ^ { 4 } } { 8 } \right) } { \left[ \frac { E W H } { L ^ { 3 } } \right] } x ^ { 3 }
$$

Where $\sigma$ is the residual fabrication-based axial stress and the other variables are previously defined. Each term in equation (5) specifically defines one part of the overall deflection of the fixed-fixed beam. The first linear coefficient deals with the residual axial stress $( \sigma )$ contribution of the stiffness. The second linear coefficient deals with the small-deflection linear stiffness with respect to its moment of inertia. In equation (5) above, as $L$ increases, the first term (residual stress term) in the stiffness equation dominates the linear stiffness. The non-linear term in $x$ deals with the stretching of the neutral axis of the fixed-fixed beam in response to the transverse deflection [13].

As discussed previously, each individual beam segment in the folded spring is not axially constrained, therefore allowed to expand, contract, and rotate, relieving any beam curvature/ residual stresses [14–16]. Therefore, the linear axial stress dependant term of the stiffness is minimized and can be ignored, reducing equation (5) to (6):

$$
F = \left\{ \left( \frac { \pi ^ { 4 } } { 6 } \right) \left[ \frac { E W H ^ { 3 } } { L ^ { 3 } } \right] \right\} x + { \left( \frac { \pi ^ { 4 } } { 8 } \right) } { \left[ \frac { E W H } { L ^ { 3 } } \right] } x ^ { 3 }
$$

If equation  (6) is examined in detail, varying the effective length of the folded spring through the number of folds, the trends shown in figure 2 are found.

As shown in figure  2, the stiffness of the folded spring (the slope of the force/displacement relation) exhibits both non-linear and quasi-linear behavior. According to [13], equation  (6) will behave linearly when the displacement of the beam is less than or equal to the thickness of the beam, or $H \lesssim x$ . This can be seen in figure 2 for deflections of less than $3 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ $( H = x )$ . As the number of folds is increased, the quasi-linear stiffness region expands above the $H \lesssim x$ linearity condition. This suggests that the quasi-linear behavior of the harvester can be increased by using a folded spring. A linear stiffness allows the natural/operational frequency of the harvester to be easily estimated, which is important for minimizing losses while matching conditioning circuitry for maximum power transfer. Furthermore, by limiting the input vibration amplitude to enforce the $H \lesssim x$ linearity condition and/or operating within the quasi-linear regime, the mechanical stiffness of a clamped-clamped beam can be reduced to equation (7) [13].

$$
k = \frac { \pi ^ { 4 } } { 6 } \bigg [ \frac { E W H ^ { 3 } } { L ^ { 3 } } \bigg ]
$$

By folding the beam, as shown in figure 3, the effective length of the beam exposed to bending is increased [13]:

The stiffness of the beam now can be expressed by equation (8) for the configuration in figure 3.

$$
k = \frac { \pi ^ { 4 } } { 6 } \bigg [ \frac { E W H ^ { 3 } } { ( L _ { \mathrm { e f f } } ) ^ { 3 } } \bigg ] = \frac { \pi ^ { 4 } } { 6 } \bigg [ \frac { E W H ^ { 3 } } { ( 3 L ) ^ { 3 } } \bigg ] = \frac { \pi ^ { 4 } } { 6 } \bigg [ \frac { E W H ^ { 3 } } { ( n L ) ^ { 3 } } \bigg ]
$$

Where $L ,$ in this case, is defined in figure  3 and $n$ is the number of beam lengths included within the folded beam structure. As can be seen from equation (8), as the number of folds of the beam is increased, the effective length increases, decreasing the overall stiffness of the beam. Equation  (8) assumes that the members joining the individual beams of the folded spring structure are rigid, undergo no appreciable bending, and only contribute to the stiffness of the structure slightly as torsional springs [13].

sections.heading: 3. Design methodology
sections.text:
In this study, the goal was to apply the folded spring structure to lower the natural frequency of the harvester while identifying the important design parameters. Two classes of folded spring energy harvesters were developed in this study, using a similar design methodology and the same fabrication and testing methodology. The two classes of folded spring energy harvester are shown schematically in figure 4:

![](images/396926dc56b8feb078820868488f33cca8a05fef12454e9b5b00dd0d84a729cf.jpg)  
Figure 3. Schematic of the folded spring showing folded and unfolded configurations. By unfolding the spring, the increase in effective bending length can be seen. Reproduced from [13] with kind permission from Springer Science and Business Media.

The Class I Energy Harvesters, as shown in figure 4, focus upon only on the folded springs that have been postulated to be a replacement elastic member for piezoelectric energy harvesters. These proof-of-concept devices allowed for the development of a universal microfabrication process for PZTbased energy harvesters and proof of design concept. The Class II Energy Harvesters, as shown in figure 4, included arrays of masses and folded spring energy harvesters to reduce the operational/natural frequency of $3 0 { - } 3 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . The secondary goal of these devices was to examine the benefits of parallel and series arrays of springs while attaining a low natural frequency.

sections.heading: 3.1. Class I energy harvesters
sections.text:
Using the folded spring concept as a basis for design, a One at A Time (OAT) sensitivity study was undertaken to identify the important parameters of the folded spring geometry in order to minimize its stiffness. The entire geometry of the harvester was parameterized into a small number of independent variables shown in figure 5.

As shown in figure  5, the entire geometry of the folded spring can be defined by four variables: three variables determining the planar geometry and a thickness of the spring. Parameter “A” defines the width of the folded spring throughout the entire length of the beam, “B” defines the gap between each beam in the fold, and “C” defines the length of the beam in the fold. To prevent unrealistic Class I Harvesters, the parameters were limited to achievable dimensions via microfabrication. The width (A) was limited between $1 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and $5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , the fold gap (B) was limited between $5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and $5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , the internal beam length was limited between $1 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and $2 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , and the thickness limited between $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ and $1 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . To save computational time only the structural silicon layer was modeled. It can be shown through a composite beam approximation that the larger thickness of the structural silicon layer of the energy harvester will dominate the bending stiffness of the structure versus the thinner metallic and piezoelectric layers. The simulation results including and excluding the thinner layers agreed within $2 \%$ error and was later experimentally verified.

![](images/9f96c3d1d676d5769ddea790d2b0d1ef9c184909a435ddd9888222ac338fb55b.jpg)  
Figure 4. The two classes of energy harvesters examined in this study. Class I Harvesters are single folded springs. A four fold spring is shown on the left; a two fold spring is shown on the right. Class II Harvesters are arrays of folded beams including at least one proof mass.

![](images/6322e774fa4ae3bb2df26b4946c3ca755608e174295d2bbf5525fd3a202dd719.jpg)  
Figure 5. Parameters used to parametrically define the geometry of the folded spring. “A” refers to the width of the beam of the folded spring, “B” is the overlap gap between each beam in the fold, and “C” is the internal length of the beam.

The OAT sensitivity study yielded several important qualitative results to help design subsequent generations of harvesters. The thickness of the folded spring was found to have the most effect on the natural frequency. The length of the beam in the fold is the second most dominant parameter of the stiffness of the folded spring. The width of the folded spring has a small effect on the stiffness and natural frequency of the folded spring. The width of the beam adds additional mass, however, in comparison to the thickness; it does not greatly affect the stiffness of the folded spring. The overlap gap of the folded spring does not affect the bending stiffness of the folded spring significantly, since this length of spring will be subject to a small amount of torsion and no appreciable bending. Using this approach, a variety of prototype single folded spring energy harvesters were designed within the above constraints, with a spring thickness of $2 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , having natural frequencies ranging from $5 1 2 \mathrm { H z }$ to $9 9 5 \mathrm { H z }$ . Additionally, it was determined in the initial structural simulation that the expected maximum stress/strain location for the folded beam was at the root of the beam. The strains encountered at the internal corners of the folded springs were generally slightly less but of the same magnitude. It is expected that the stress concentrations at the internal corners of the beam will be relaxed due to design fidelity loss during fabrication.

![](images/6aab7b59771dcac7a218de3b5dedf13c0ebe95dc89b8adb81e412c45cb69f358.jpg)  
Figure 6. Schematic of series and parallel arrangements of folded springs and masses and normal and rotated oriented folded springs.

sections.heading: 3.2. Class II harvesters
sections.text:
The second class of energy harvesters examined in this study built upon the characterization Class I Harvesters, adding masses and arrays of harvesting elements to further drive down the natural frequency of the energy harvester. In this class of energy harvester, there were five major design parameters that were examined: the number of folds in the flexible element, the number of masses and flexible elements in the array, the configuration of the flexible elements, the orientation of the flexible elements, and the thickness of the spring elements. An optimized folded spring design is used from the previous work, in both a two-fold/four-fold configuration. The masses and springs were arranged in parallel and series configurations to allow for a wider variety of designs and applications. The parallel designs allowed for a good balance between stability and natural frequency reduction to allow for higher acceleration load applications. The series designs allowed for the further natural frequency reduction through addition of additional masses and spring elements. The additional spring elements in series acted similarly to adding folds to a single folded spring, increasing the effective bending length. Examples of series and parallel arrangements are shown in figure 6. Table 1. The orientation of the spring elements were varied in order to take advantage of both out of plane and rotational motion of the proof mass. The normal orientation of folded spring, as shown in the left of figure 6, will allow for the mass to oscillate in an out of the plane of the harvester. The individual beam elements will undergo mostly bending in this orientation of the spring element. The rotated orientation as shown in the right of figure 6, will allow for the masses to mostly rotate, rather than oscillating in and out of plane. The rotation of the mass, in this case, causes the individual beam elements of the folded spring to undergo bending. It was expected that the rotated orientation folded spring devices will be mechanically stiffer than the normal orientation folded spring devices, allowing for higher amplitude accelerations/larger suspended masses. As with the Class I Harvesters, the thickness of the spring elements was varied in order to create a wide range of natural frequencies with the same planar design. The permutations of these parameters filled the design space, as shown in table 1. These designs were numerically analyzed in order to compare the frequency spectrum of these designs with the experimental results of the microfabricated Class II Harvesters. The comparison of the experimental and simulated natural frequency of each design of harvester versus the spring thickness will be examined in detail in the results section of this paper.

sections.heading: 4.1. Microfabrication of the energy harvesters
sections.text:
The piezoelectric energy harvester requires a piezoelectric thin film to convert the strain created through the displacement of the harvester into electricity. There are three materials that can be used as thin films for this application, Lead Zirconate Titanate (PZT), Zinc Oxide, and Aluminum Nitride [1, 22]. In literature, PZT is dominantly used for power generation purposes. Zinc Oxide and Aluminum Nitride are more commonly used in actuation and sensing. In general, the piezoelectric coefficients for a variety of PZT materials are much higher in magnitude than Aluminum Nitride and Zinc Oxide [1, 22]. For 31-mode energy harvesters (beam-bending based), higher ${ \bf d } _ { 3 1 }$ piezoelectric coefficients are desirable [23]. Additionally, the variety of PZT materials and deposition technologies allow for greater control over both the material properties and deposition thicknesses of the PZT film. This is important for the thickness dependant material properties of the PZT, such as the relative permittivity, that may vary significantly over a few hundreds of nanometers of thickness [24]. Although there have been recent advances in using Aluminum Nitride in microgeneration applications [12], PZT will be the primary piezoelectric material used.

The sol-gel PZT deposition process required a repetitive spin-bake-anneal cycle to build up the thickness of the film. The sol-gel was spun and then baked on a hot plate three times sequentially to build up a film thickness of approximately $0 . 2 4 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The film was annealed at $7 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to crystallize the PZT. This process can be repeated to build up additional PZT thickness in steps of $0 . 2 4 \mu \mathrm { m }$ per cycle. The PZT material was characterized with X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) to ensure that the material was crystallizing properly.

To accommodate the PZT film, the energy harvester required a variety of materials for adhesion and electrical isolation. For adhesion of PZT to a silicon wafer, silicon dioxide, a titanium-based layer, and a platinum layer were required [22]. Silicon dioxide was required as an adhesion layer for the titanium-based layer and as an electrical insulation layer to prevent charge leakage into the silicon substrate. A titaniumbased layer was required to allow the platinum layer to adhere to the silicon oxide layer. Titanium and titanium tungsten are both valid options, depending upon the processing required to pattern/crystallize the PZT material used. During crystallization anneals, titanium may diffuse into the silicon/silicon oxide creating a titanium silicide at a high temperature [25], which may cause delamination at PZT thicknesses of more than one deposition cycle ${ \mathrm { 0 . 2 4 } } \mu { \mathrm { m } }$ thick) of sol-gel. To prevent this behaviour, a more diffusion-resistant film, such as titanium tungsten, was required. The platinum was required as an adhesion/electrode/seed layer for the PZT film. The required arrangement of layers produced a specific stack of materials shown in figure 11. In addition, these layers must be patterned in a stepped profile in order to prevent short circuiting of the bottom and top electrodes. With this general harvester design, the microfabrication process shown in figure 7 was developed.

The microfabrication process begins with a double side polished ${ < } 1 0 0 >$ silicon wafer with silicon oxide grown onto it. The titanium/titanium tungsten and platinum layers were patterned via a lift-off procedure. The silicon oxide layer was patterned by photolithography and then etched via a buffered oxide wet etch. The PZT material was deposited on the wafer using the sol-gel deposition method and etched using a multistep wet etch. The platinum top electrode was deposited by lift off, following the same procedure as the previous platinum layer. The structural release of the harvesters involved two sequential DRIE etch steps. The first etch defined the planar geometry of the harvesters on the front side of the wafer. The second DRIE process etched deep wells on the backside of the wafer. This DRIE etch required the use of a carrier wafer to prevent wafer fracture and handling issues due to the global thinning of the wafer during the etch. The intersection of the two deep silicon etches released and defined the geometry of the energy harvesters.

sections.heading: 4.2. Packaging of the energy harvesters
sections.text:
The energy harvesters were characterized under a base excitation; therefore it was not possible to directly probe the energy harvesters in a typical probing station. The entire harvester would move in and out of the contact with the electrical probes, thereby preventing the continual capture of the output electrical signal. Therefore, it was necessary to package the harvester onto printed circuit boards (PCB) to enable in-situ characterization. As seen in figure 8, Solid PCB’s were designed to package individual harvesters. In order to allow free vibration, a hole was punched in the PCB for each proof mass. The prepared PCB allowed for the direct mounting of a harvester chip with an acrylocynate glue, without spacers, reducing the required handling and potential for damage.

After the harvester was adhered to the PCB, the harvester is electrically connected to the PCB via a ball-wedge gold wirebond and then to the outside world via soldered wires. This method of packaging has been proven not to add a parasitic capacitance. This specific packaging scheme was used for both classes of energy harvesters examined in this study. Examples of packaged harvesters can be seen in figure 8.

sections.heading: 5. Characterization and testing methodology
sections.text:
The general characterization and testing methodology used in evaluating both classes of harvesters produced in this study is shown in figure 9.

The harvesters are initially characterized to evaluate the performance of the individual microfabrication processes. The harvesters are then packaged to provide the necessary electrical connections for testing equipment. The frequency response of the harvester is measured using a Laser Doppler Vibrometer (LDV). Finally, the electrical performance of the harvester is tested by applying a known vibration and measuring the electrical output of the harvester. As seen in figure 9, the results of the testing and characterization, positive or negative, are used to revise the designs and microfabrication processes to improve the microfabrication and device performance.

![](images/be550f00e8a23d776ef398c43c0b059935eb142da136dcf63aa7b8365d096c25.jpg)  
Figure 9. Schematic of the characterization and testing methodology. The testing and characterization provides a feedback loop to the design/microfabrication process to diagnose and correct device-based problems.

sections.heading: 5.1. Microfabrication characterization
sections.text: The initial characterization of the harvesters focused on evaluating the microfabrication processes used to produce the energy harvesters. The microfabrication recipe was validated and tested to ensure that the recipe was producing operational piezoelectric energy harvesters. Thickness measurements and surface profiles were taken by profilometry and scanning electron microscopy in order to ensure proper film thicknesses, continuous films, and that electrical shorting was not occurring. Characterization of the microfabrication processes throughout the development of the microfabrication recipe has been essential in fabrication development.

sections.heading: 5.2. Vibration testing
sections.text: The vibration testing of the piezoelectric energy harvester focused on capturing the frequency response of the harvester in response to a base excitation. This involved applying a base excitation to the harvester with a mechanical shaker and recording the resulting vibration with a LDV. In order to measure the response of the energy harvester, one may apply either a pseudo random or a harmonic frequency sweep input vibration signal. The Doppler shift of the reflected laser light was measured by the LDV, allowing for the out of plane velocity of the energy harvester to be captured in real time. A Fast Fourier Transform of the velocity profile is taken to determine the frequency spectrum of the harvester. To determine the frequency response of the harvester alone, two separate measurements were required—the frequency response of the harvester and the shaker system itself. In order to remove the response of the shaker from the energy harvester, the frequency spectrum of the harvester must be normalized by the frequency spectrum of the shaker. This normalization filters the noise/dynamics of the base motion from the dynamics of the harvester, leaving only the frequency spectrum of the target energy harvester [26].

sections.heading: 5.3. Electrical testing
sections.text:
Initially, the harvesters were checked for short circuits. A shorted harvester would not produce an output signal, since the voltage produced across the film would be instantly equalized via the short. This was typically caused by pinholes and non-continuous PZT films allowing the upper and lower electrodes to contact. The non-shorted harvesters had their capacitance measured in the next characterization step. The piezoelectric stack in this device produced a capacitor, with PZT as the dielectric material. The capacitance of the harvesters were measured and then used to verify the conversion of vibration to electricity. The input impedance of the harvester was calculated from the measured capacitance at rest and the operational/natural frequency of the specific harvester. The input impedance of the harvester was then used to compare against the optimum load resistance for maximum power transfer, at the operational/natural frequency, to verify vibration-electricity conversion.

![](images/4c11a5b359bbebd39a1c982fc4e00e4282c7de6b9817324368c4907484a653b8.jpg)  
Figure 10. Experimental frequency response of an example Class I Harvester. Experimentally measured natural frequencies of $\omega _ { \mathrm { l } } = 1 8 7 0 \mathrm { H z }$ and $\omega _ { 2 } = 3 4 2 3 \mathrm { H z }$ . Design natural frequencies of $\omega _ { \mathrm { n 1 } } = 1 9 1 0 \mathrm { H z }$ and $\omega _ { \mathrm { n } 2 } = 3 4 6 7 \mathrm { H z }$ .

The first vibration-based electrical test undertaken on the harvester was to identify the optimum load resistance upon which the maximum power transfer was attained. For this test, low amplitude acceleration vibrations at the natural frequency of the harvester were applied by the mechanical shaker. As the load resistance of the circuit was varied, it was possible to determine the optimum load resistance that allows maximum power transfer. According to the maximum power transfer theorem, input impedance and the optimum load resistance should be equal to allow for maximum power transfer [27]. When these two values coincided, it was clear that the harvester was converting vibration to electricity.

Once the harvester was confirmed to be operational, the acceleration applied to the harvester was increased in order to evaluate the harvesting potential of the design. This included applying known input vibrations, either sinusoidal or other measured waveforms from potential applications, to the harvester.

sections.heading: 6.1. Class I Harvesters
sections.text:
The Class I Harvesters were packaged and integrated as discussed in the above packaging section. The in-depth characterization has shown that the numerical predictions and experimental frequency response of these devices were in agreement, showing that the mechanical design intent of the folded spring energy harvesters was intact. An example of this correlation for a sample Class I Harvester is shown in figure 10.

The measured natural frequency of the harvester, captured at $1 8 7 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , was close to the simulated design natural frequency of $1 9 1 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Although the second measured natural frequency at $3 4 2 3 \mathrm { H z }$ appears to be the dominant frequency of the system, the normalization required to remove the base dynamics of the testing equipment distorted the magnitudes of the resonant peaks. The velocity response of the device was on the same order of magnitude as the base/background dynamics, therefore the normalization can distort the results. This was one of the major motivations of adding masses to the Class II Harvester designs.

![](images/bfeb5f70147bb06a5689675f44d54d2bb29821afbfe507d6ba70853d6e6a6802.jpg)  
Figure 11. SEM image of the corner of the folded spring, illustrating the thickness and cross section of the folded spring.

The experimental and calculated natural frequency for the Class I Harvester shown in figure  10 agree within approximately $4 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , or ${ \sim } 2 \%$ . There are several factors contributing to the offset between the design and measured natural frequencies. For example, the silicon wafers used to fabricate the Class I Harvesters had a thickness variation of approximately $\pm 1 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , causing a standard deviation of $3 . 2 5 \mathrm { - } 5 . 4 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ in folded spring thickness after the DRIE etch steps. Additionally, the etch processes used to define the cross section of the folded spring also did not produce a truly rectangular cross sectioned beam, degrading the design intent, as shown in figure 11.

As the DRIE etch depth increases, the isotropy of the repeated cyclic etch causes the sidewalls of the well to be progressively more etched. This undercut of the harvester imposes a trapezoidal cross section  onto the beams, which reduces the moment of inertia, mass, and stiffness of the folded spring. Using the moment of inertia of a trapezoidal cross section and equation (8), the effect of this undercut can be seen in figure 12.

As can be seen in figure 12, the loss of stiffness behaves non-linearly as the cross section transitions from rectangular to triangular. At the absolute extreme, this behavior can cause upwards of $6 6 . 6 \%$ stiffness loss at a complete undercut. The mass loss of the harvester is linear according to the loss of cross sectional area. The overall change in natural frequency due to the undercutting, as seen in figure 12, is small until the undercut becomes more pronounced, around $40 \%$ undercut. Depending on the depth of etches undertaken in the release for a specific harvester, this microfabrication-based deviation from the design intent could account for a significant portion of offset error between the calculated and measured natural frequencies.

The characterized Class I Harvesters has validated the initial simulation work. The measured and calculated natural frequencies agree, for the example in figure 10 by ${ \sim } 2 \%$ , with the major sources of error identified and quantified. Additionally, the characterization has suggested that the methodology to lower the natural frequency of the harvester using folded springs is valid and warrants the additional exploration with Class II Harvesters. Additionally, the harvester did not exhibit any of the symptoms of residual stress-based beam curling, suggesting that the folded beams are insensitive to the residual stress produced through microfabrication.

![](images/b3f164417afd2506d313211c5ce1d8700c2899497d01758d04fcf53ff10f1e04.jpg)  
Figure 12. The effect of the undercut from the DRIE process on the spring stiffness, mass and natural frequency of the energy harvester.

A number of prototype devices were electrically characterized using a sinusoidal input acceleration signal of $1 9 . 6 2 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { \Omega }$ $\mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ at a frequency of $1 2 \mathrm { H z }$ . This harsh loading was required to actuate the harvesters sufficiently enough to produce a measurable output signal. Using a conditioning circuit to increase the resolution of the output signal of the energy harvester, it was possible to produce a power output of approximately $1 0 . 9 0 \mathrm { n W } .$ . Since the harvester was driven far from its natural frequency by necessity of applying a large acceleration to deform the structure, the output power achieved was fairly low. As this was a proof of concept device, the presence of a measurable output signal allowed for the more complex designs of the Class II Harvesters to be pursued.

sections.heading: 6.2. Class II Harvesters
sections.text:
The Class II Harvesters were packaged and integrated using the packaging scheme previously discussed. The released Class II Harvesters did not exhibit any symptoms of fabricationbased residual stresses, such as beam curling, mass rotation, or distortion of the harvester design at rest, confirming the residual stress relaxation of the folded spring-based design. The frequency response of the Class II Harvesters was characterized using the previously discussed methodology. The studied harvesters had folded spring thicknesses varying from $1 9 . 8 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ to $7 6 . 6 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ over eleven separate fabricated wafers of Class II Harvesters.

In the following figures, the simulated and experimentally measured natural frequencies for a variety of harvester designs will be compared. For each figure, the simulated range of natural frequencies includes an upper and lower bound of natural frequencies based on the variation of proof mass due to wafer thickness variation $( 5 1 0 \mu \mathrm { m } ~ \pm ~ 1 5 \mu \mathrm { m } )$ . The expected natural frequency from the harvester examined should occur within the simulation range created by these bounds. Additionally, it was not possible to directly correlate the natural frequency measured from a specific harvester to its specific folded beam thickness. To directly measure the thickness of the folded spring of a specific harvester, the device would have to be broken post measurement to allow for a SEM image to be taken perpendicular to the thickness of the spring. Due to this limitation, the average and standard deviation of the measured thickness achieved from each wafer with the corresponding natural frequency measurements were used to show the most probable region where the measurements would be expected. For the discussions below, this area will be referred to as the “error area” of each design. In cases of only one surviving harvester per design/wafer, a single point with error bars representing the standard deviation of folded spring thickness is shown.

As shown in figure 13, Design A spanned natural frequencies from $2 7 7 . 9 \mathrm { H z }$ to $2 3 2 7 \mathrm { H z }$ .

The experimental and simulated natural frequencies of the Design A harvester correlated well for most trials of spring thickness examined. The range of experimentally measured points fell within the expected natural frequency range for most of the spring thickness domain. The Design A harvesters from thicker folded spring wafers, such as MS2P6, seemed to have more variability in natural frequency, causing the overall trend of experimental measurements to deviate from the simulated expected range. Taking into account the increased variability of the results from MS2P6, the correlation of the experimental and simulated results suggest that the simulation and design methodology are validated for this design.

Design B, as shown in figure  14, is of similar scale to Design A, but utilizes rotated folded springs spanning natural frequencies from $3 1 9 . 6 \mathrm { H z }$ to $2 5 4 5 \mathrm { H z }$ .

As expected, Design B with the rotated folded springs was slightly stiffer than Design A with the normal orientation design. The polynomial fit of the experimental measurements follows the same general trend of the simulation. The individual frequency measurements from each wafer are a bit more scattered in proximity to the polynomial fit, producing a lower coefficient of determination. Although the data points are a bit more scattered than in Design A, the all of the error areas from each wafer, except MS2P8, are in close proximity to the expected results from simulation, with some bias offset. Given the variability of the frequency response results from the polynomial fit, the general trend of the polynomial fit suggests trend agreement between the simulation and experimental results of this design.

As shown in figure 15, Design C spanned natural frequencies from $1 3 7 . 3 \mathrm { H z }$ to $5 8 7 . 3 \mathrm { H z }$ over the range of tested wafers.

It is clear that the larger mass and additional folds applied to Design C, in comparison to Design A, additionally reduced the natural frequency with a small increase in footprint. Only one harvester from MS2P3, with folded spring thickness of $2 5 . 2 6 \mu \mathrm { m }$ survived packaging and testing. The samples from MS2P4, with beam thicknesses of $1 9 . 8 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , were not mechanically stable for Design C. From figure 15, it can be seen that the clusters of data from each wafer correlate well to the polynomial fit. Additionally, the polynomial fit follows the same general trend as the simulated response of the design with a bias error. The general trend of the fit, when coupled with the correlation of the data points, suggests that there is a common trend between the experimental and simulated results.

![](images/7f3fc0a349ee0f14ddb54fd8c79799a13ed67184a1edd98b5a066c886467d8a0.jpg)  
Figure 13. Comparison of natural frequency versus folded spring thickness for both simulations and experiments for Design A.

![](images/1e9f595b6556c9b247d0438a2f28fadd5d55cae4be7cbc227aad19a4e2bdcb9b.jpg)  
Figure 14. Comparison of natural frequency versus folded spring thickness for both simulations and experiments for Design B.

As shown in figure 16, Design D spanned natural frequencies from $1 1 8 . 1 \mathrm { H z }$ to $6 6 0 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ over the range of tested wafers.

It is clear that the larger mass and additional folds applied to Design D, in comparison to Design B, additionally reduced the natural frequency with a small increase in footprint. The samples from MS2P4, with beam thicknesses of $1 9 . 8 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , were not mechanically stable for Design D. With stiffer rotated springs, Design D was capable of producing devices from MS2P3, allowing for the natural frequency span of this design to be slightly larger than Design C. This suggests that the rotated folded springs may allow for a targeted balance between stability and natural frequency reduction. From figure  16, it can be seen that the clusters of data from each wafer correlate well to the polynomial fit. The polynomial fit follows the same general trend as the simulated response of the design with a bias error, as was the case with Design C. The general trend of the fit, when coupled with the correlation of the data points, suggests that there is a common trend between the experimental and simulated results.

As shown in figure 17, Design E spanned natural frequencies from $9 5 . 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ to $8 5 6 . 6 \mathrm { H z }$ over the fabricated wafers.

Design E further extended the stiffness reduction from Design A by adding an additional mass and spring element in series. The additional folded spring element in series cumulatively added to the effective bending length of the structure, driving the natural frequency range of the design downward significantly. The stability limit of the structure due to thickness was not reached with these expanded designs, as was seen with Designs C and D, therefore, it may be possible to further reduce the thickness of the folded springs in these devices to further drive down the natural frequency. The experimental data agreed well with the simulation results. Error areas from all wafers overlapped the simulation range of natural frequencies expected. The polynomial fit had a strong correlation to the experimental data and showed the same general trend as the simulations with a small bias offset. These factors suggest that the simulation and experimental work agree for this design of harvester.

![](images/68ef23cdd4d80dd9eab23f9a367da79ca0b819b9248f1964ecb540d6ddd4cf37.jpg)  
Figure 15. Comparison of natural frequency versus folded spring thickness for both simulations and experiments for Design C.

![](images/62b8b634267f4f6c1c22953fe51f765df5d96971478d645c17128ee35439a663.jpg)  
Figure 16. Comparison of natural frequency versus folded spring thickness for both simulations and experiments for Design D.

As shown in figure 18, Design F spanned natural frequencies from $1 1 9 . 6 \mathrm { H z }$ to $9 9 9 . 3 \mathrm { H z }$ over the range of folded spring thicknesses produced.

This design built upon Design B by adding an additional mass and spring element in series. The additional folded spring element in series cumulatively added to the effective bending length of the structure, driving the natural frequency range of both designs downward significantly. As previously with Design E, the stability limit due to thickness was not reached with Design F harvesters, therefore, it may be possible to further reduce the thickness of the folded springs in these devices to further drive down the natural frequency. Similarly to Design E, there is a strong correlation for the experimental data to the simulated range of natural frequencies expected for all groups of Design F harvesters, except those from MS2LO2. Taking the behavior of MS2LO2 into account, the strong correlation of both the polynomial fit and the experimental data to the simulated range of expected natural frequencies suggests that the experimental work and simulation agree for this design of harvester.

![](images/d6c7f17973ee30da29677a0f1463905bcf9c6c0348598724d47c25c53896b8d6.jpg)  
Figure 17. Comparison of natural frequency versus folded spring thickness for both simulations and experiments for Design E.

![](images/defa4b0d1fc9571ce4a4a736e2475f9bf7a075b441fd3ce26f719bf046a49fd4.jpg)  
Figure 18. Comparison of natural frequency versus folded spring thickness for both simulations and experiments for Design F.

As shown in figure 19, Design G was capable of spanning natural frequencies from $4 5 . 2 1 \mathrm { H z }$ to $2 0 7 . 9 \mathrm { H z }$ for the harvesters produced.

Design G was the largest footprint design in the study and the lowest natural frequency range. As with the less mechanically stiff design iterations, the maximum frequency reduction was limited by the mechanical stability of the fabricated harvesters. As with Design C, Design G did not have any functioning devices from MS2P3 or MS2P4. This was expected, since the evolution from Design C to Design G was the addition of an additional mass and spring element in series, thereby producing a heavier and less stiff structure. The data captured from the tested harvesters correlated well with the polynomial fit, however, as with Designs C and D, a bias error occurred. As with the other designs, the harvesters produced with Design G yielded lower natural frequencies than expected by the simulations. The general trend of the fit, when coupled with the correlation of the data points, suggests that there is a common trend between the experimental and simulated results.

![](images/227a75c7793c11a2d46845e5dbc29bfc1f4c7355f7eba08f332d28d3a9f75985.jpg)  
Figure 19. Comparison of natural frequency versus folded spring thickness for both simulations and experiments for Design G.

![](images/c91d3b6591b9f8cd934e0b5652aa705b498369c592b96622152691275b5935a0.jpg)  
Figure 20. Comparison of natural frequency versus folded spring thickness for both simulations and experiments for Design I.

As shown in figure 20, Design I spanned natural frequencies from $4 2 0 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ to $3 1 3 2 \mathrm { H z }$ for the range of fabricated harvesters.

As can be seen in the figure, the experimental data points agree fairly well to the simulated range of expected natural frequencies. The error areas of every wafer of harvesters overlaps the range of expected natural frequencies. Additionally, the polynomial fit of the experimental data agrees well with the simulated range of expected natural frequencies. The strong agreement of the data to the simulated range of expected natural frequencies suggests that the simulation work is valid for this design.

As shown in figure 21, Design J spanned natural frequencies from $3 3 6 . 0 \mathrm { H z }$ to $3 6 6 7 \mathrm { H z }$ for the folded spring thicknesses of harvesters fabricated.

Design I and Design J were parallel configurations of springs and a single mass that produced a large, mechanically stable, range of natural frequencies over the range of achieved thicknesses. As expected, the rotated folded spring orientation in Design J was slightly more mechanically stiff, resulting in higher comparative natural frequencies. As seen in figure 21, the experimental data and the simulated range of expected natural frequencies have somewhat of a correlation, with error areas overlapping the simulation range. However, the polynomial fit of the data suggests that a bias error exists between the experimental data and the simulation, with the simulation overestimating the natural frequency. The general trend of the fit, when coupled with the correlation of the data points, suggests that there is a common trend between the experimental and simulated results.

![](images/f4bcfd07551f9921e0e69b33fdd16dceceb8a1e0c1ca74cacde3bca386e51af2.jpg)  
Figure 21. Comparison of natural frequency versus folded spring thickness for both simulations and experiments for Design J.

![](images/0f4c6b1f8094045791f4bc08da7fe32080fe0e3d8bf3d2ae1a91a484dfb9d658.jpg)  
Figure 22. Comparison of natural frequency versus folded spring thickness for both simulations and experiments for Design K.

As shown in figure  22, Design K spanned natural frequencies from $8 0 . 6 3 \mathrm { H z }$ to $8 3 2 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ for the harvesters tested in this study.

This design scaled up Design I by adding additional mass volume and folds to the folded springs. This drove down the natural frequency range in comparison to the smaller footprint design. The experimental data has some correlation to the simulated range of natural frequency, with overlapping error areas for most of the wafers tested. As with other designs, the harvesters from MS2P6 have a large variability in natural frequency. The high variability in MS2P6 is confined only to that set of harvesters. Additionally, this variability causes the polynomial fit of the data to be somewhat distorted at near the MS2P6 data set. Although the specific experimental data points correlate to the expected simulation range, the bias error suggests a similar trend only.

![](images/346c82f932078bbcbe9057b96f9575dd5ccb2f53eba3e2b1b368158c9b9e3f69.jpg)  
Figure 23. Comparison of natural frequency versus folded spring thickness for both simulations and experiments for Design L.

As shown in figure 23, Design L spanned natural frequencies from $1 0 8 . 1 \mathrm { H z }$ to $9 5 4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ for the range of harvesters produced.

This design scaled up Design J by adding additional mass and folds to the folded springs. This drove down the natural frequency range in comparison to the smaller footprint design. The experimental data points correlate with the simulation range, with overlapping error areas with all designs of harvester, except MS2LO2. The polynomial fit correlates well with the experimental data, however, has a bias offset to the simulated data. Although the specific experimental data points correlate to the expected simulation range, the bias error suggests a similar trend only.

The bias error between the simulated and measured natural frequencies encountered over the various designs of harvesters was not contained to a specific subset of designs—it occurred, to some degree with every design. It was more prevalent with Designs C, D, G, J, K, and L, therefore it was not linked to a specific spring orientation or arrangement of harvester. According to Dixit et al. [28], the local etch rate of a DRIE process is dependent on the available surface area. Areas of larger open surface area will etch faster than smaller open surface areas. Designs C, D, G, J, K, and L have the largest open surface area backside wells of all the designs produced in this study. This suggests that these devices will be comparatively thinner than the average thickness measured from the devices on the same wafer. This overestimation of the true thickness of the harvesters for this design would cause the bias error seen in the comparisons. Therefore, the designs affected by the areadependant etch variation, having suitable experimental trend behavior matching the simulation trends with a bias offset also verify the simulation and design work. The correlation of the simulation and experimental results suggests that the effect of the microfabrication residual stresses on the stiffness of the harvesters was small and that the linear approximation of the folded spring stiffness made by equation (8) is valid. This will allow for certainty in matching the frequency and input impedance/load resistance requirements of specific applications, moving forward with new designs and optimization of these more complex systems.

![](images/770294bc564488d3c997ea5b7c1ec6db97bf1176810ff2a48b73ed8837326cda.jpg)  
Figure 24. Natural frequency ranges of all designs compared to the target frequency range of $3 0 { - } 3 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . All designs except Designs B, I, and J are capable of meeting this requirement in this work.

In general, it was seen that the normal orientation folded springs are less mechanically stiff than the rotated folded springs. The proof mass placement in the studied designs suits normal orientation springs, since a higher degree of bending can be applied to the individual beam elements with the same loading. It was found that the arrangement of the centrally aligned rotated folded springs and masses did not allow for a significant amount of rotation of the proof mass, causing a lower degree of bending to be applied to the individual beam elements in the rotated folded springs. The bending could be enhanced for the rotated folded springs by offsetting the centroid of the proof masses from the midline of the folded springs. As expected, the designs with the four-fold springs had much lower natural frequencies than the two-fold systems. This was due to the larger effective length of the beam. The series systems have much lower natural frequencies the parallel systems, however, tend to be more fragile. The additional effective beam length that can be accomplished through series systems is limited by mechanical stability of the harvester design. Beyond manipulating the design and creating a new mask set, manipulating the thickness of these devices will have the greatest impact on their natural frequency. Both the footprint and device thickness can be chosen to optimize the mechanical performance of the harvester to a specific target application. If there are few constraints on the footprint of the intended harvester, a seriesbased harvester utilizing more than one mass (Designs E, F, and G) could be used to fill this role with a large device thickness. This would allow the device to be actuated at the appropriate frequency, while being mechanically robust. If the available footprint of the harvester is limited, then the overall thickness of the device would need to be reduced to allow sufficient frequency reduction. In this case, either a single mass seriesbased design (Designs A, B, C, or D) or a parallel-based system (Designs J-L) would be the most appropriate. The thinning of the devices for these designs has less of an adverse effect on the mechanical robustness of these harvesters, allowing for target natural frequencies to be achieved in a smaller footprint.

When the entire design space is compared with the target natural frequency range of $3 0 { - } 3 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ to harvest low frequency vibration, it was seen in figure 24 that most of the designs were capable of satisfying the requirement.

As seen in figure 24, the designs that were not capable of meeting the goal natural frequency range are Designs B, I, and J. Design A was only partially capable of meeting the $3 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ requirement, while the rest of the designs were capable of meeting the majority of the target frequency range. Designs A, B, I, and J would be able to meet this target frequency range easily at a reduced spring thickness, further suggesting that the examined designs of folded spring harvesters are capable of harvesting low frequency vibrations.

The capacitance of each non-shorted harvester element was measured in order to calculate the internal impedance of the harvesters. Four harvester element footprints were used throughout the eleven designs; therefore, similar capacitances will occur across different designs of the harvester, given a consistent PZT thickness, as shown in table 2.

To verify vibration-to-electricity conversion, the optimum load resistance of the harvesters was determined. The devices were actuated in the linear regime by a low amplitude vibration at their natural frequency. By measuring the root mean squared voltage across the load resistance, it was possible to capture the power output the harvester produced as the load resistance was varied, as seen in figures 25 and 26.

As expected, for the three example harvesters examined above, the optimum load resistance for maximum power output was consistent for each individual harvester. In the experiments, the input vibrations applied to the harvesters were specifically chosen to be very low, in the “sub-g” range, from $0 . 3 \mathrm { m m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ to $7 0 \mathrm { m m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ to ensure that the operation of the harvester stays within the quasi-linear range. Additionally, as expected, the output power increased as the acceleration applied to the harvester was increased.

When the optimum load resistances were compared to the input impedance calculated from the capacitance measurements in previous testing, it was seen that the input impedances and optimum load resistances were well correlated. The input impedance and optimum load resistance, as shown in figures 25 and 26 coincided at $5 3 . 8 6 \mathrm { k } \varOmega$ for Device C1, $2 2 . 4 5 \mathrm { k } \varOmega$ for Device L1, and $1 2 . 0 2 \mathrm { k }varOmega$ for Device I2. This correlation of the input impedance of the energy harvester and the optimum load resistance of the conditioning circuit suggests that the harvesters are converting vibration to electricity in a predictable manner as designed.

Once it was confirmed that the harvesters were operating correctly, the input acceleration near resonance was increased to $9 . 8 1 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ . Measurements were then taken using the appropriate optimum load resistance to determine a maximum power transfer possible from the harvesters. For this experiment, a sinusoidal acceleration was applied to the harvester. A sample of power output measurements for single harvesting elements of each harvester are summarized in table 3, showing the natural frequency at which the harvester was excited, the input impedance, the measured RMS voltage across the load resistance, and the calculated RMS current and average power produced by the harvester.

As seen in table  3, the harvesters are able to produce a reasonable power output near resonance. The largest power output achieved in this study was approximately $6 9 0 . 5 \mathrm { n W }$ of power at a RMS voltage of $1 5 3 \mathrm { m V }$ and RMS current of $4 . 3 2 \mu \mathrm { A }$ across the optimum load resistance, while operating at its natural frequency of $2 2 6 . 3 \mathrm { H z }$ at $9 . 8 1 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ . Although this power output is not as high as some comparable devices in literature, the power output for the thickness of PZT film used in these harvesters $( 0 . 2 4 \mu \mathrm { m } )$ was reasonable, producing a comparable energy density of approximately $5 4 \mu \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ . There were some titanium-based adhesion challenges encountered were encountered in producing PZT films thicker than $0 . 2 4 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , which necessitated the use of a titanium tungsten adhesion film. PZT films as thick as $0 . 9 6 \mu \mathrm { m }$ have been produced in microfabrication tests, however, have not yet been applied to the folded spring harvesters. The increased PZT thickness will result in an increase of power output, according to equation (1). Taking into account the effect of the increased PZT thickness, the resulting power output can be estimated. Based on the result in table 3, if Device C2 had a PZT thickness of $0 . 9 6 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , its natural frequency would remain unchanged, the input impedance would increase to $1 0 0 . 9 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , the output RMS voltage would increase to $5 2 7 . 8 \mathrm { m V } , \quad$ the output RMS current would increase to $5 . 2 3 \mu \mathrm { A }$ , and the output power would increase to $2 . 7 6 \mu \mathrm { W }$ . As can be seen by this estimation, the increase in output voltage far outweighs the increase in output current for the increase in PZT thickness. This is due to the increase in input impedance due to the change in relative permittivity in response to the PZT thickness. In addition, with the use of the inherent arrays of harvesting elements in the Class II Harvester designs, it will be possible to additionally increase the overall power output of the harvester.

sections.heading: 7. Conclusions
sections.text: In this paper, a folded spring-based harvester was presented as an alternative to the traditional cantilever-based piezoelectric harvester to reduce the natural/operational frequency to the range of human motion. Multiple designs of folded spring energy harvesters have been designed, produced and tested. The Class I Harvesters produced in this study demonstrated that the design methodology discussed in this work of reducing the natural frequency of the harvesters was sound. Additionally, to produce the Class I Harvesters, a robust and flexible microfabrication process was developed. This process and knowledge gained was then applied to the Class II Harvesters which introduced an additional reduction of natural frequency using arrays of folded spring harvesting elements and proof masses. This methodology allowed for a wide frequency bandwidth of vibration to be captured, from $4 5 \mathrm { H z }$ to $3 6 6 7 \mathrm { H z }$ , over a variety of harvester designs. The Class II Harvesters were shown experimentally to be insensitive to stiffness changes due to residual stresses that may be produced through the microfabrication of the harvester—a major obstacle for beam-based piezoelectric harvesters. The use of a folded spring, in this case, increased the quasi-linear range of the harvester, allowing for the correct match of load resistance without potential drift and losses due to nonlinear spring stiffening. The Class II Harvesters, utilizing the folded spring harvesting elements, were confirmed to convert input vibration into electricity. The maximum power output of the current compliment of Class II Harvesters was $6 9 0 . 5 \mathrm { n W }$ at $2 2 6 . 3 \mathrm { H z }$ for a single harvesting element, with a PZT layer thickness of $0 . 2 4 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . Increased thickness PZT films have been achieved in microfabrication tests, and will be applied to subsequent harvester designs in order to further increase power output. The work undertaken in this study demonstrates that the fixed-fixed folded spring can be used as a viable structural element for low frequency piezoelectric energy harvesting to take advantage of ambient vibrations found in human-based motion.
